newsitem.title: USA: U.S. proposes barring Sun-Diamond affiliates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes barring Sun-Diamond affiliates.

text.p: The Agriculture Department Friday proposed barring the affiliates of the California fruit group Sun-Diamond Growers from federal food contracts after its recent criminal conviction for giving illegal gifts to a former Clinton cabinet member.

Sun-Diamond was convicted in September in a federal court on eight criminal counts that included illegal gratuities to former Agricuture Secretary Mike Espy in 1993 and 1994 and illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry.

The charges arose out of the government's two-year special investigation of the former Agriculture Secretary, who resigned in 1994 amid accusations he took illegal gifts and favours from companies the department regulated.
In October, the department barred Sun-Diamond from selling products to the government for the next three years. McBride said the company has appealed that ruling.

The department on Friday chided Sun-Diamond's five affiliates, which rank as the nation's largest raisin, prune, walnut, fig and apricot cooperatives, for their "silence" about business practices that led to the conviction. It also proposed a dozen top Sun-Diamond officials be excluded from contracts.

"USDA proposes to debar Sun-Diamond's directors, managing officials, and affiliates because of their silence and failure to correct the criminal and dishonest business practices leading to the court conviction," the department said in a statement.

The move could mean millions of dollars in lost sales for the cooperatives. Over the past six years, the department has bought about $15 million worth of raisins, prunes, figs and walnuts from the growers, largely for the school lunch programme, department data shows.
Any ban would extend to all federal food purchase programmes, such as those supplying the military and prisons.
Sun-Diamond, based in Pleasanton, Calif., expressed disappointment with the department's action and said it would appeal within the 30 days alloted.

"The cooperatives and their officers hold themselves to the highest ethical standards," said Sun-Diamond communications manager Sandra McBride. She noted the proposed debarment did not affect contracts currently in place.

The affiliates targeted by the department are Diamond Walnut Growers Inc., Stockton, Calif.; Sun-Maid Growers of California, Kingsburg, Calif.; Sunsweet Growers Inc., Yuba City, Calif.; Valley Fig Growers, Fresno, Calif., and Hazelnut Growers of Oregon, Cornelius, Ore. Also on the list was Sun-Diamond packaging subsidiary Sunland Products of California.
Sun-Diamond is owned by the five grower groups, which are in turn owned by about 4,500 farmers. The affiliates have not been named in any criminal indictments.
The department did not specify how long it sought to debar the affiliates but said a typical ban extends for three years.
